identity.name: The Advocate
identity.tag: No seat. No vote. Everything else.
identity.desc: You lead the campaign for tax fairness — the coalition outside the building, the argument inside it. Members carry the bills; you make them impossible to ignore.

intel._note: The weekly intel report. Each FACET is gated by the skill that would really buy it: Whip Count prices the chairs (live scheduling odds — rumor below `band`, honest band at `band`, exact odds + disposition at `exact`), Procedure reads the clock (deadline warnings before they are one week out), Fiscal Acumen puts the MEASURED hearing rate in print (it is always in the bill tooltip, but tooltips don't exist on touch). Rumor-tier odds are seeded per week+bill and may be off by one band — wrong on purpose; do not 'fix' the noise.

poles._note: Display grouping for the skill sheet — Disco groups skills under their parent attribute and colors them by it; ours group under the campaign function they serve. Order here is the order they render, and each pole's color lives in CSS as .p-<id>.

_skillsNote: skills.*.pole is WONK (inside/institutional), ORGANIZER (outside/movement) or BRIDGE (works both faces — pure metadata today, not read by any code; grouping/UI is a later step). Fiscal + Procedure are wonk; Rhetoric + Grassroots are organizer; Talk Story + Whip Count are bridge. Clean 2/2/2 on purpose. NOTE: this note lives OUTSIDE the skills object on purpose — main.js does `Object.keys(data.skills)` to enumerate skill records, so a stray key INSIDE skills breaks every skill-grid render (learned the hard way, 2026-08-13).

fiscal.name: Fiscal Acumen
fiscal.desc: Revenue estimates, fiscal notes, and whether the number on the page is real.

procedure.name: Procedure
procedure.desc: Referrals, deadlines, decking — what the rules quietly allow.

whip.name: Whip Count
whip.desc: Who's really with you — in the building, and in the coalition.

rhetoric.name: Rhetoric
rhetoric.desc: Hearings, cameras, and the sentence people repeat afterward.

talkstory.name: Talk Story
talkstory.desc: Reading a person — a skeptical chair or a coalition partner, same skill either way.

grassroots.name: Grassroots
grassroots.desc: Coalition capacity — how many people you actually turn out, and how fast.

rally.name: Hold a rally
rally.desc: Pack the rotunda. Sign-waving, testimony trainings, kūpuna in matching shirts.

scale._note: Grassroots turns the SAME rally into a bigger, cheaper one — more support per point of skill, less political cost. Reuses the identical skill/per math as check mods (modOf), just applied to an action's effects instead of a roll.

rally.result: The rotunda echoes for an hour. A senator's aide films it from the balcony, expressionless. Coverage runs at six and ten.

voices.text: THIS is the building's real acoustics test. Let them hear who the budget is for.
Noise is not arithmetic. The people upstairs vote on arithmetic. Usually.

lobby.name: Work the building
lobby.desc: Office to office, floor by floor. Coffee, one-pagers, favors remembered.
lobby.result: Four offices, two commitments, one 'send me the language.' The building runs on exactly this.

voices.text: Quiet rooms. Reasonable voices. This is where taxes get trimmed into something survivable.
Fine — but count who's already IN those quiet rooms every day. It isn't the folks from the rally.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Session opens Wednesday. Here's the picture: the Council on Revenues says $9.8 billion in general-fund taxes next year. The budget spends $10.6 billion of general funds. The gap is savings and prayer. You don't hold a seat in that building — what you hold is the campaign: the coalition, the argument, and members willing to carry your bills. Whatever you hand them this week IS your session — so choose like it.

voices.text: A gap means the wealthiest state economy in the Pacific is UNDERTAXED at the top. You know the list: conveyance, capital gains, the loopholes. Hand them all of it.
A gap means spending grew faster than a shrinking tax base. Families are already paying the highest cost of living in America. Hand them restraint.

choices.label: "We lead with the kids — meals, credits. Then we show how to pay for it."
choices.reply: Nālani nods once. "Then the revenue bills aren't optional. They're the ending of the story you just picked."

choices.label: "We lead with the math. Nothing moves unless it balances."
choices.reply: "The money chairs will love you," she says. "The coalition will want to know the math includes people."

choices.label: Say nothing. Look at the numbers again.
choices.reply: She waits. The numbers do not improve under observation. "Okay. Pick the package — the calendar won't."

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Ground rules while it's quiet. Each week you get the room — talk to whoever you want — and ONE real move: a rally or a walk through the building. And what you spend your weeks doing, you get better at doing. Weeks disappear faster than you think. Lateral, crossover, conference, gone.

voices.text: One move a week. Scarcity. Finally, a mechanic this campaign understands.
Then never waste it on a week where nobody's watching.

choices.label: "Understood."
choices.reply: "Good. Sleep this week. You won't later."

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Opening Day. Lei on every railing, three governors in the gallery — and the press set up on the makai steps, where your campaign has the 9 a.m. slot. One microphone, four minutes, every outlet in town. What's the message?

voices.text: Say the quiet number LOUD: seventy percent of capital gains go to people making over $400K. Four minutes is plenty.
Say nothing a chair has to answer for by lunch. Thank the members carrying your bills, praise the kūpuna, hand out the one-pager.

choices.label: "Tax fairness, by name. The register pays more than the penthouse."
choices.reply: The crowd claps. Upstairs, two office doors close quietly. Grange, at the edge of the steps, writes one word on a legal pad.

choices.label: "Cost of living. Discipline. A budget that doesn't wobble."
choices.reply: Inside, the murmurs are approving. Somewhere on the sidewalk, a coalition text thread goes quiet.

choices.label: Four minutes of pure aloha — thank everyone, promise nothing.
choices.reply: Warm, safe, forgettable. Three offices call before lunch asking for 'whatever that one-pager was.'

start.speaker: fonoti
start.text: Fonoti doesn't look up from the committee referral sheet. "I schedule what can pass. The bills your people are carrying — I can hear one of them early, IF the ask is trimmed to something the floor survives. Or you keep the full number and wait for me to find a week. Maybe I find one."

voices.text: Take the trim. A smaller bill that PASSES beats a poster that dies in committee.
The 'trim' is how a hundred million becomes a press release. Make him find the week.
He said 'find a week.' Weeks are HIS. But a chair who names a date in front of a witness has spent something he can't unspend.

choices.label: Trim the ask. Get the early hearing.
choices.reply: "Smart." He initials the sheet. Your bill just got $25M/yr lighter — and a hearing date.

choices.label: Hold the number. "Find the week, chair."
choices.reply: A long pause. "Bold." It is not clear that 'bold' is a compliment on this floor.

choices.label: "Name the date, chair. In front of Nālani."

success.reply: He looks at Nālani, then at you, and writes a date on the referral sheet in pen. "February 14th. Don't make me regret the ink."

failure.reply: "In front of staff?" The sheet goes face-down. "I'll find a week." He will not find a week.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: Grange finds you by the koa doors, all smiles. "Big session, yeah? Our members can live with a lot — but the conveyance thing reads like a tax on selling your own house. Help me help you: carve out everything under three million, we stay neutral. Testify friendly, even."

voices.text: Neutral-to-friendly from the roundtable is worth actual votes. Carve-outs are the price of oxygen here.
The bill ALREADY exempts normal homes — that's the design. He's negotiating against a version that doesn't exist. Say so. Smile back.

choices.label: "It already exempts owner-occupied homes. Read the bill, Curtis."
choices.reply: The smile holds, one degree cooler. "Then our testimony will read the bill very... closely."

choices.label: "Send me your carve-out language. No promises."
choices.reply: "That's all I ask." It is never all he asks.

choices.label: "Say it at the hearing, then. On the record, under your own name."

success.reply: The smile finally goes. "We don't usually testify on the record this early." They don't testify at all. Your bill gets a hearing without a villain in the room.

failure.reply: "Happy to!" And he does — warmly, at length, in favor of a version of your bill that does not exist. The committee writes down HIS number.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Rumor from the tax department: the Council on Revenues may shave the forecast at its next meeting. If it's true, every bill with a price tag gets harder. The coalition wants to know the campaign's posture before the papers ask.

voices.text: A softer forecast is the floor telling you the ceiling is lower. Get ahead of it: pause the spending bills, look prudent.
A softer forecast is the ARGUMENT for revenue bills. You don't fix a leak by drinking less water.
'May shave the forecast' is not a number. Somewhere there is a worksheet with a number on it. Ask for the worksheet.

choices.label: Go public first: "This is exactly why we fix revenue."
choices.reply: You beat the rumor to the microphone. The clip travels. So does your name, attached to the word 'taxes.'

choices.label: Brief the steering committee quietly. Keep powder dry.
choices.reply: Doors close, voices lower. The building notices a campaign that can keep its own counsel.

choices.label: Say nothing yet. Ask the department for the actual worksheet.

success.reply: Three pages of tables. The shave is 0.4 percent, not the two the rumor grew on the way over. You walk into the steering meeting with the real number and watch the room recalibrate around you.

failure.reply: You quote a line from the wrong column at the wrong meeting. It is corrected, gently, by someone junior to you.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Health department's in the hallway with a real one: a federal reimbursement fell through and a rural clinic network needs a $40M emergency appropriation to stay open through the fiscal year. The rescue coalition wants your campaign's name on the joint letter by Friday.

voices.text: Forty million to keep clinics open in places with one doctor per island district. This is what the general fund is FOR.
Every 'emergency' signed in February is a structural deficit by June. Where exactly is the forty coming from?

choices.label: Sign the letter. Clinics stay open.
choices.reply: Your campaign's name goes second on the list. The clinic director cries in the hallway. The fiscal note does not.

choices.label: Ask for a scrubbed budget first. Defer.
choices.reply: Prudent, defensible — and the neighbor-island papers run 'LAWMAKERS STALL CLINIC RESCUE' anyway.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Morning paper, page A1 turn: an op-ed titled 'The Last Tax Hike Hawaiʻi Can Afford,' signed by three retired executives. It names your bills. It is, annoyingly, well written.

voices.text: They're not wrong about the cost of living. They're only wrong about who's causing it. Which is... a nuance op-eds reward.
Three retired executives against school meals. Print THAT sentence and you win the week.

choices.label: Write the response yourself. Name the stakes, name the kids.
choices.reply: Your reply runs Sunday. The coalition shares it 400 times. One executive writes again; nobody reads the sequel.

choices.label: Let it breathe. Op-eds don't vote.
choices.reply: By Thursday it's fish wrap. The building respects a campaign that doesn't chase every ball.

choices.label: Skip the reply. Take it to live radio, unedited.

success.reply: Forty minutes, no filter, one host who lets you finish a sentence. By noon two of the three executives are being asked about THEIR taxes.

failure.reply: You are asked, four times, whether this is a tax increase. Four times you explain that it is complicated. The clip that travels is the fourth time.

start.speaker: malia
start.text: Hearing day. Malia's got forty testifiers signed up — teachers, a school cook, two ranchers, a hotel housekeeper with her whole shift outside. Two minutes each. The chair is already checking his watch. She asks: who leads?

voices.text: The cook. Nobody explains a food budget like the person who stretches one for four hundred kids.
The ranchers. When the committee hears 'small business supports this,' the math gets a passport.

choices.label: The school cook goes first.
choices.reply: Two minutes, no notes. The chair stops checking his watch. Twitter does the rest.

choices.label: The ranchers go first.
choices.reply: 'We're not anti-business — we ARE the business.' Two committee skeptics visibly recalibrate.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Friday coalition potluck, church hall two blocks makai of the Capitol. Someone brought squid lūʻau, someone brought Costco chicken bake, and somebody's cousin on Senate staff brought a rumor about conference chairs. Attendance is, technically, optional.

voices.text: Half the real appropriations of the decade were settled over paper plates. Go. Bring something store-bought and humble.
Go — but talk story with the STAFF. They know which bills are actually moving. Also the squid lūʻau will be gone by 12:15.

choices.label: Go. Eat. Listen twice as much as you talk.
choices.reply: You learn two referral rumors and one recipe. The week ends warmer than it started.

choices.label: Skip it. The inbox is a crime scene.
choices.reply: Productive, lonely. Monday, everyone else shares an inside joke about the chicken bake.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: Sine die. Lei on the podiums again, and the building exhales all at once. Whatever you moved this session is moving; whatever you didn't is next January's problem. Interim starts tomorrow — that's when we count what it all did.

voices.text: Rest. Then back to it — the gap doesn't adjourn.
Adequate. Nobody bankrupted the place, which around here counts as a triumph.

choices.label: Walk out through the rotunda one more time.
choices.reply: The Capitol is open to the sky in the middle — by design. Money in, money out, and the weather gets a vote too.

start.speaker: nalani
start.text: "Status check: your bills are alive until a deadline says otherwise. Watch the calendar chips — lateral and crossover weeks are where bills go to die quietly. Spend your action where a week actually turns."

voices.text: She schedules your optimism. Keep her.

choices.label: "Thanks. Back to it."
choices.reply: "Drink water. Sessions are cardio."

start.speaker: fonoti
start.text: "Every advocate who makes it up these stairs thinks their bill is the one the ceiling bends for." He taps the referral sheet. "Bring me something the floor survives, and we'll talk about ceilings."

voices.text: The ceiling is a CHOICE. Someone typed it into a spreadsheet.
The man guards the arithmetic. You will need him more than he needs you.

choices.label: "Noted, chair."
choices.reply: He almost smiles. Almost.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: "Nothing personal, ever — that's the first rule of this hallway." He offers macadamia candy from a tin. "Our members just want predictability. Tax bills are weather. We sell umbrellas."

voices.text: Predictability IS worth money. He's the most honest person on this floor, in the way a price tag is honest.
Take the candy. Audit the metaphor. Weather doesn't hire three lobbyists per raindrop.

choices.label: Take the candy. Keep walking.
choices.reply: It's good candy. It is always good candy.

start.speaker: malia
start.text: "The coalition count: 61 orgs on the meals bill, 40 on the credit, 'it's complicated' on everything with the word conveyance. We can turn out bodies for one big moment per month — tell me early which moment matters."

voices.text: This is your actual caucus. The one that shows up in matching shirts.
Sixty-one organizations, one shared printer. Respect the logistics.

choices.label: "You'll get two weeks' notice. Promise."
choices.reply: "Two weeks is luxury. Deal."

choices.label: "Forget my calendar. What does the coalition actually need?"

success.reply: She stops doing math on her phone. "Somebody to not disappear in April." Then, quieter, the real list — three things, none of which are a rally.

failure.reply: "Bodies at a hearing, like I said." She goes back to her phone. You asked a real question in a hallway, which is where real questions go to be small talk.
